qa.name: Serratus Posterior Superior
qa.origin: Inferior part of ligamentum nuchae; spinous processes of C7–T3 and their supraspinous ligaments
qa.insertion: Superior borders of ribs 2–5, just lateral to their angles
qa.function: Elevates ribs 2–5 during forced inspiration; assists in expanding the thoracic cavity
qa.clinical_note: Serratus Posterior Superior appears in both the thoracic wall group (VH Dissector classification) and the Back — Intermediate region (Moore's extrinsic back muscle classification). This dual placement reflects its transitional position — it originates from the posterior neck and upper thoracic spine but acts on the anterior rib cage. It lies deep to the rhomboids. Its primary role is respiratory — elevating the upper ribs during forced inspiration. Clinically implicated in myofascial pain of the upper back.

qa.name: Serratus Posterior Inferior
qa.origin: Spinous processes of T11–L2 and their supraspinous ligaments; thoracolumbar fascia
qa.insertion: Inferior borders of ribs 9–12, just lateral to their angles
qa.function: Depresses and fixes ribs 9–12 during forced expiration; counteracts the upward pull of the diaphragm on the lower ribs
qa.clinical_note: Serratus Posterior Inferior appears in both the thoracic wall group (VH Dissector) and Back — Intermediate (Moore). It lies deep to latissimus dorsi. Its role is to anchor the lower ribs during forced expiration and coughing — acting as a counterforce to the diaphragm. Together with Serratus Posterior Superior they are sometimes called the accessory muscles of respiration. Both are thin muscles that can be difficult to distinguish from underlying aponeuroses on dissection.

qa.name: Levatores Costarum
qa.insertion: Outer surface of the rib immediately below (Levatores Costarum Breves); or 2 ribs below (Levatores Costarum Longi)
qa.innervation: Posterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves (T1–T11)
qa.function: Elevates the ribs assisting inspiration; lateral flexion and extension of the vertebral column
qa.clinical_note: Levatores Costarum appear in both the thoracic wall group (VH Dissector) and Back — Deep: Short Segmental (Moore's minor deep intrinsic layer). VH Dissector groups them here because of their direct action on the ribs. There are 12 fan-shaped muscles, one at each thoracic level. The short form (Breves) inserts one rib below; the long form (Longi) skips a rib. Innervated by posterior rami — notable as one of the few posterior rami muscles with a direct effect on rib movement.

qa.name: External Intercostals
qa.insertion: Superior border of the rib below; fibers run downward and forward. Replaced anteriorly by the external intercostal membrane
qa.innervation: Intercostal nerves (anterior rami of T1–T11); outermost intercostal layer
qa.function: Elevates the ribs during inspiration; increases anteroposterior and transverse diameters of the thorax
qa.blood_supply: Posterior intercostal arteries; anterior intercostal arteries
qa.clinical_note: The three intercostal layers from external to internal are: External Intercostals, Internal Intercostals, Innermost Intercostals. The intercostal neurovascular bundle (VAN — vein, artery, nerve, superior to inferior) runs between the internal and innermost layers in the costal groove. Always insert a chest drain above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. External intercostal fibers run downward and forward — like hands in front pockets. Replaced anteriorly by the external intercostal membrane between costal cartilages.

qa.name: Internal Intercostals
qa.origin: Superior border of each rib and costal cartilage; costal groove
qa.insertion: Inferior border of the rib above; fibers run upward and forward, perpendicular to external intercostals. Replaced posteriorly by the internal intercostal membrane
qa.innervation: Intercostal nerves (anterior rami of T1–T11); middle intercostal layer
qa.function: Interosseous part: depresses ribs during forced expiration. Interchondral part: may assist elevation of costal cartilages during inspiration
qa.clinical_note: Internal intercostal fibers run upward and forward — like hands in back pockets — at right angles to the external intercostals. The intercostal neurovascular bundle (VAN) travels in the costal groove deep to the internal intercostals and superficial to the innermost intercostals. The internal intercostals extend from sternum to vertebral column, unlike the external intercostals which are replaced anteriorly by membrane. This layer is incised during thoracotomy. Intercostal nerve block targets the space between internal and innermost layers.

qa.name: Innermost Intercostals
qa.origin: Inner surface of ribs; occupy the middle half of each intercostal space
qa.insertion: Inner surface of the adjacent rib above; fibers run in same direction as internal intercostals
qa.innervation: Intercostal nerves (anterior rami of T1–T11); innermost intercostal layer
qa.function: Depresses ribs; acts with internal intercostals during forced expiration
qa.clinical_note: The innermost intercostals are the deepest of the three intercostal layers and are separated from the internal intercostals by the intercostal neurovascular bundle (VAN — vein, artery, nerve). They are part of the same muscle sheet as Transversus Thoracis anteriorly and subcostals posteriorly. The intercostal nerve block is placed in the costal groove between internal and innermost intercostal layers — making knowledge of this layer essential for regional anaesthesia and chest drain insertion.

qa.name: Transversus Thoracis
qa.origin: Posterior surface of the lower sternum and xiphoid process
qa.insertion: Inner surfaces of costal cartilages of ribs 2–6
qa.function: Depresses costal cartilages of ribs 2–6; assists in forced expiration
qa.clinical_note: Transversus Thoracis (also called Sternocostalis) lies on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall and is considered the anterior continuation of the innermost intercostal layer. It is a key surgical landmark in coronary artery bypass grafting — the internal thoracic (mammary) artery runs immediately deep to it and is harvested as a conduit. VH Dissector groups it with the thoracic wall muscles. Moore considers it part of the same innermost layer as the innermost intercostals and subcostals.

qa.name: Diaphragm
qa.origin: Sternal part: posterior surface of xiphoid process. Costal part: inner surfaces of costal cartilages and adjacent bony surfaces of ribs 7–12. Lumbar part: right and left crura from bodies of L1–L3 (right) and L1–L2 (left); medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
qa.insertion: Central tendon — a trefoil-shaped aponeurosis with no bony insertion
qa.innervation: Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) for motor and central sensory; lower intercostal nerves (T6–T12) for peripheral sensory only
qa.function: Primary muscle of inspiration — contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure. Also increases intra-abdominal pressure during defecation, micturition, and parturition
qa.opposing_muscle: Abdominal muscles (raise diaphragm during forced expiration)
qa.blood_supply: Superior and inferior phrenic arteries; musculophrenic artery; pericardiacophrenic artery
qa.clinical_note: Three major openings: aortic hiatus (T12 — aorta, azygos vein, thoracic duct), oesophageal hiatus (T10 — oesophagus, vagal trunks), caval foramen (T8 — IVC). Mnemonic: 'I 8 (ate) 10 eggs At 12' — IVC T8, Oesophagus T10, Aorta T12. Motor innervation exclusively from the phrenic nerve — 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'. Referred shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation (subphrenic abscess, ruptured spleen) travels via phrenic nerve to C3–C5 dermatomes. Hiatus hernia involves herniation through the oesophageal hiatus.
